core_sections: How Wrela differs from Rust and TypeScript
brief:
You're writing a program in wrela, a new programming language for games, to measure how learnable it is. Read these files first, and only these (no other files in the repository: not the compiler, its tests or its standard library sources): {context}.

Your task ({id}): {task}

Every program is a package: a directory whose entry file is `main.wrela`. Yours is {dir}/pkg; write your files there. Every program must export `pub fn frame(time: f32, width: u32, height: u32)`, called by the host once per frame (its body may be empty when the task has no GPU work), unless the task gives it the program's state.

To compile, run exactly `{attempt} {dir}`: it builds the package, records the attempt and prints the compiler's diagnostics. You may also run `{wrela} doc <item>`, `{wrela} explain <code>` and `{wrela} primer [area]` to look things up. Don't run the compiler any other way. Write your whole first version before you compile it. You have at most {max_attempts} attempts. Every attempt is graded by hidden tests of the exports the task names, so a program that builds but doesn't do what the task says counts as wrong: stop when it builds and you are confident it does what the task says.

When you're done, report: (1) whether it built, and on which attempt; (2) for each attempt that didn't build, each diagnostic's code, what you took it to mean, and what you changed in response; (3) anything in the language or its documentation that misled you.
